standard: Crosswalk — EU / UK / US refund & return obligations
source: Curated mapping of public consumer-protection frameworks

obligations.title: EU ↔ UK alignment (post-Brexit retained rights)
obligations.body: The UK retained the core of the EU Consumer Rights Directive via the Consumer Rights Act 2015 and the Consumer Contracts Regulations 2013. Both grant a 14-day cancellation right for distance/online sales and a tiered refund/remedy structure, so an EU-style return policy maps closely to UK obligations — but sellers serving both markets should disclose each regime explicitly and not rely on a single 'EU' label.

obligations.title: Card-scheme chargeback ≠ statutory refund right
obligations.body: Visa/Mastercard chargeback is a payment-network dispute remedy, NOT a substitute for statutory refund rights (EU 14-day withdrawal, UK 30-day rejection, US state law). A compliant return policy must honour the statutory right first; the card-scheme path is a backstop when a merchant fails to refund. Never tell a customer a chargeback is their 'only' option where statute grants a direct refund.

obligations.title: US federal floor + state supplements (e.g. California ARL)
obligations.body: The FTC sets a federal baseline (Cooling-Off Rule, truthful advertising) but does NOT grant a general 14-day e-commerce return right — that comes from seller policy or state law. States like California add stronger protections (Automatic Renewal Law). US return/refund copy must state the seller's own policy clearly and not imply a federal statutory return right that does not exist for ordinary online sales.
